Zebedee
zeb'ē-dē
n. (a fisherman of Galilee, husband of Salome and father of the apostles James and John, left in the ship with the hired servants when his sons were called)
Greek Zebedaios, from Hebrew Zabdi or Zebadyah, the LORD hath given or gift of the LORD, from zabad, to bestow. The name is a confession, and the man was asked to give back exactly what the name says he had received.

Biblical Definition

Zebedee is named eleven times in the Gospels and speaks not once. He is a Galilean fisherman of some substance — his boat carried hired servants as well as family — and he was at work with his sons when Christ came along the shore: “he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them” (Mat 4:21). The next verse is the whole of the man's trial in eleven words: “And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him” (Mat 4:22). Mark adds the detail that softens nothing: “they left their father Zebedee in the ship with the hired servants, and went after him” (Mar 1:20). Luke shows the family was in partnership with Simon (Luk 5:10), so a going business lost half its young men in an afternoon. His wife Salome followed Christ, ministered to Him of her substance, came asking for thrones for her boys (Mat 20:20), and stood at the cross. His sons became the Sons of Thunder (Mar 3:17), and one of them was the first apostle martyred (Act 12:2) while the other outlived them all. Of Zebedee himself, Scripture records the nets, the hired servants, and the silence.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Zebedee; in sacred history he is a fisherman of Galilee, the father of the apostles James and John.

ZEBEDEE, n. The gift of the LORD; a proper name in the Greek Scriptures.

A fisherman of Galilee, the husband of Salome and father of James and John.

He was mending his nets in the ship when our Saviour called his two sons.

His trade employed hired servants, and was in partnership with Simon Peter.

He is named often as the father, but no word of his is recorded.

Key Scripture

Mat 4:21 — "And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them."

Mat 4:22 — "And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him."

Mar 1:20 — "And straightway he called them: and they left their father Zebedee in the ship with the hired servants, and went after him."

Mar 10:35 — "And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, come unto him, saying, Master, we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire."

Modern Corruption

Modern devotional writing turns Zebedee into a study in the emotional cost of ministry to families. The Gospels present the call of his sons as the absolute claim of Christ, which is a harder thing and a better one.

expand to see more

It is now common to read Mark 1:20 through the lens of family systems — the father abandoned, the business disrupted, the unprocessed grief of the man left in the boat. The instinct is not entirely wrong; Scripture never pretends discipleship is costless, and Zebedee is put in the text precisely so the reader feels the weight of the two sons walking away. But the therapeutic frame changes the subject. Mark is not describing a family crisis; he is describing what happens when the Son of God calls a man, and the hired servants are mentioned to show the reader that Christ's claim does not wait on a succession plan.

The Lord said it plainly enough: “He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Mat 10:37), and He also said, promising the return, that no man has left house or brethren or father for His sake “But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time” (Mar 10:30). Both stand. The fifth commandment is not repealed by the call — John took the mother of Jesus into his own home at the cross, which is a son honouring a parent while hanging on for the kingdom. What the frame of trauma cannot supply is the accounting Christ Himself gives: the boat was worth losing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Zebedaios (G2199), Zebedee; ploion (G4143), ship, boat; misthōtos (G3411), hired servant; katartizō (G2675), to mend, to make fully ready; akoloutheō (G190), to follow.

expand to see more

Greek Zebedaios (G2199) — Zebedee; from the Hebrew, the LORD hath given.

Greek ploion (G4143) — ship; the working boat he was left sitting in.

Greek misthōtos (G3411) — hired servant; the mark of a business of some size.

Greek katartizō (G2675) — to mend, to fit thoroughly; the nets, and later the saints.

Greek akoloutheō (G190) — to follow; the one verb the sons obeyed.

Usage

"“In a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets” — an ordinary morning before the call."

"“They left their father Zebedee in the ship with the hired servants” — the cost stated without comment."

"“The mother of Zebedee's children” — the household named by the man who never speaks."
